overview: Oceania Healthcare is a New Zealand-listed operator of 37 retirement villages and aged care centres, accommodating approximately 3,900 residents and employing around 2,700 staff across sites from Ruakaka in the north to Riccarton in the south. The business generates value through a dual-segment model: selling Occupation Right Agreements (ORAs) across 2,003 independent living units and 1,090 premium care suites, while earning recurring income from government-funded and premium-pay care operations across 1,068 traditional care beds. Under new CEO Suzanne Dvorak (appointed July 2024), Oceania is executing a turnaround focused on sales performance, cost optimisation, and balance sheet repair ahead of a FY27-FY31 growth phase.

business_model.summary: Oceania operates the Occupation Right Agreement (ORA) model common to NZ retirement village operators, combined with a differentiated 'care premiumisation' strategy. Residents pay a lump-sum ORA price for the right to occupy an independent living unit or care suite; upon departure, Oceania retains a Deferred Management Fee (DMF) of roughly 25-30% and replenishes the ORA for resale. This creates a capital recycling engine. The care segment earns government-subsidised fees for standard care beds and charges Premium Accommodation Charges (PACs) or care suite DMFs for higher-acuity premium care. Development of new villages generates one-time development margins (c.35% currently) on new sales.

revenue_streams.name: Care Operations (beds & care suites)
revenue_streams.notes: FY25 care revenue NZD $200.3m (77% of operating revenue). Includes government-funded beds, PAC fees, and care suite DMF accrual. Care EBITDA per bed rising sharply (+45.5% HoH to $12.4k in 1HY26).

revenue_streams.name: Village Operations (ILU weekly fees & DMF accrual)
revenue_streams.notes: FY25 village revenue NZD $52.4m (20% of operating revenue). Weekly service fees plus accrued DMF over occupancy period.

revenue_streams.name: Other / Corporate (incl. former Wesley Institute)
revenue_streams.notes: Wesley Institute of Nursing Education closed April 2025 (contributed ~$4.7m EBITDA in FY25). Future corporate costs expected to fall ~20% after headcount right-sizing.

business_model.key_cash_flows: ORA receipts (cash received on new sales and resales) are the primary cash generation driver - FY25 ORA receipts were NZD $294.5m (+30% on FY24), the largest lever to repay development debt. Operating cash flow FY25: $110.3m (+6.7% YoY). 1HY26 operating cash flow: $79.0m (+12.2% HoH).
business_model.customer_type: B2C - residents 75+ years seeking independent retirement living or residential aged care. Mix of government-subsidised (means-tested) and privately-funded ('self-pay') residents. Oceania targets the premium segment, particularly with its care suite product and The Helier luxury offering.
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand only. Portfolio skewed to Auckland (key development sites: The Helier, Franklin, Lady Allum, Meadowbank, Waterford, Elmwood) plus major regional centres (Hamilton, Tauranga, Christchurch, Hawkes Bay, Nelson/Blenheim, Northland).

main_competitors: Ryman Healthcare (RYM.NZ) - largest NZ operator, ~49 villages, NZ and Australia
Summerset Group (SUM.NZ) - second largest NZ operator, ~37 villages
Arvida Group (ARV.NZ) - merged with Bupa NZ retirement villages; significant NZ operator
Bupa New Zealand - private (UK-listed parent), large care home operator
Metlifecare (private, owned by EQT) - premium Auckland-focused operator
competitive_position.market_position: Third or fourth largest NZ retirement village operator by unit count, with 2,003 ILUs and 1,090 care suites. Differentiated by integrated care-retirement model and premium care suite innovation. Smaller than Ryman and Summerset but larger than most private operators.

moat_factors.description: Oceania's combined retirement living and aged care offering under one roof creates stickiness - residents can age in place from independent living through dementia care without relocating. The Nurse Practitioner Model (operating in ~20 centres) and Fundamentals of Care framework reinforce clinical differentiation.

Oceania pioneered the care suite model in NZ (premium private-pay care accommodation with ORA structure), creating higher per-bed revenue and shifting exposure from government funding to private-pay. Care suite development margins running at ~35% in 1HY26.

Land bank of approximately 1,000 gross units across Auckland, Northland, Hawkes Bay and other regions, including greenfield site at Franklin. Provides optionality for 100-150 units per year development once gearing is reduced.

37 sites and 3,900 residents creates purchasing scale and operational leverage. Care resident NPS of 41 reflects decent but not exceptional satisfaction. Brand less premium than Ryman or Metlifecare currently.

Care centre certification from Te Whatu Ora (Health NZ) creates regulatory barriers to entry for new care operators. Existing operational licences and established resident relationships are difficult for competitors to replicate quickly.

weaknesses: Smaller scale than Ryman and Summerset limits cost efficiencies and brand power
Elevated debt levels (gearing 34.8% in 1HY26 vs target 30-35%) constrain development capacity
High proportion of government-funded care beds creates funding risk and margin pressure
The Helier luxury development in Auckland has materially underperformed original sell-down expectations, tying up ~$90m in unsold development stock
No Australian presence limits growth runway compared to Ryman
Corporate cost base historically too high relative to revenue; rightsizing underway
Market capitalisation below book value of net assets as at March 2025, reflecting investor scepticism about NTA realisation

growth_drivers: NZ demographic tailwind: Population aged 75+ projected to almost double by 2048-2050 (from ~414,000 to 810,000+), driving structural demand for retirement and care accommodation. NZ faces a projected shortage of 12,000 residential care beds by 2032.

Care premiumisation strategy: Shift from government-funded care beds to private-pay care suites dramatically improves revenue and margin per bed. Care EBITDA per bed rising from $8.5k (1HY25) to $12.4k (1HY26, +45.5%), with management targeting continued improvement.

FY27-FY31 strategic growth phase: Following the current foundation-building period, management plans to scale development to 100-150 units per year, focused on capital-efficient villa products at greenfield sites (Franklin Stage 2+, Lady Allum, Elmwood, Bream Bay) with target c.16% cash returns.
Cost-out programme: $20.4m in annualised savings identified, with $4.0m realised in 1HY26 and $13.2m on track for full FY26. Full benefits in FY27 are expected to significantly lift NPAT margins.
Divestment of non-core assets: Programme targeting ~$40m capital release from four additional site divestments in FY26, reducing debt and freeing capital for higher-return uses.

Sell-down of development stock: Unsold development stock reduced from $342m (FY25) to $302m (1HY26). Each dollar of sales directly reduces the development loan, improving gearing and interest coverage.

NZ interest rate tailwinds: RBNZ cut OCR to 2.25% (November 2025), reducing financing costs on bank debt (current average 4.07% on bank debt). Lower rates also support NZ property market and resident ability to afford ORAs.

Dividend resumption: New dividend policy (40-60% of Free Cash Flow from Operations) expected to attract income-focused investors once positive FCF from operations is achieved, potentially in 2HY26 or FY27.
Aged care funding increases: Budget 2025 provided an additional $1.37bn per annum from 2025/26 for aged residential care, providing relief for the government-funded segment.

business.description: NZD $302m in unsold development stock as at 30 September 2025 (c.$90m at The Helier alone). Failure to sell down this stock at target prices would delay debt reduction and pressure gearing covenants. The Helier has been the most problematic, with only 54.5% occupied/under application as at November 2025 (targeting full cash recovery by March-May 2026).

Retirement village ORA prices are partly correlated with NZ house prices. Purchasers often fund ORA entry from house sale proceeds. A sustained property market downturn would suppress demand, slow ORA resales, and compress development margins. Despite rate cuts, 2026 house price growth forecasts are modest (2-5%).

Net debt of $609m (1HY26), gearing 34.8%. Total drawn facilities $618m against $725m limits, with only $116m headroom. ICR covenant 2.5x vs 2.0x minimum. Development loan of $288m drawn against $315m facility is nearly fully drawn. Any sustained sales slowdown could threaten covenant compliance.

Care revenue depends on regulated government subsidies. Historically, government funding has lagged cost inflation, squeezing margins for traditional care bed operators. While Budget 2025 provided a $1.37bn per annum uplift, ongoing underfunding risk remains. Oceania is strategically pivoting away from beds toward private-pay care suites to reduce this exposure.

Ryman and Summerset are well-capitalised competitors with stronger brands in many markets. Summerset's 97% resident satisfaction and Ryman's vertically-integrated scale create competitive pressure. Oversupply risk exists in certain Auckland apartment sub-markets (e.g., The Helier premium segment).

New CEO Suzanne Dvorak joined July 2024 and has rapidly restructured the business. New Chief Sales & Marketing Officer (November 2024) and elevated Clinical and Sales functions to executive level. Cultural transformation and strategy execution risk exists with significant leadership change across multiple functions simultaneously.

financial.description: Oceania has $393m in bank debt (general and development facilities) at variable rates (current average 4.07%). If RBNZ were to resume rate hikes, interest costs would rise. Fixed rate $225m retail bonds (2.7% blended) expire FY28 and FY29, creating refinancing risk at potentially higher rates.
NZD-only operations; no material currency risk.

Market capitalisation trades below stated net tangible assets (NTA per share $1.57 at 1HY26 vs share price c.$0.83 as at analysis date), implying the market discounts the carrying value of property assets or expects sustained underperformance relative to NTA. This discount limits equity capital-raising options.

regulatory.description: NZ Government is reviewing the Retirement Villages Act 2003, with Cabinet decisions expected November-December 2025 and an amendment bill potentially introduced in July 2026. Key proposals include mandatory buyback periods (paying residents/families while waiting for ORA to resell), improved transparency, and enhanced dispute resolution. A mandatory buyback requirement could materially increase working capital requirements and reduce the capital efficiency of the ORA model for all operators, including Oceania. Oceania has engaged in submissions advocating for reforms that improve transparency while maintaining sector viability.

regulatory.risk: Health NZ certification and regulatory compliance
regulatory.description: Care centre operations require certification from Te Whatu Ora (Health NZ). Regulatory reform in November 2025 introduced stricter quality standards and higher staffing ratios. Non-compliance with care standards can result in certification removal, materially impacting care segment revenue. Oceania invests heavily in its Fundamentals of Care framework and Nurse Practitioner Model to maintain compliance and quality.

A Ministerial Advisory Group is reviewing aged care funding models. Potential changes to means-testing, contributions from self-paying residents, or funding model structure could affect the mix between government-subsidised and private-pay residents, impacting Oceania's care revenue mix.

macro.risk: NZ economic conditions and consumer confidence
macro.description: NZ emerged from recession in late 2024 / early 2025 with RBNZ cutting OCR from 5.5% to 2.25% through 2025. Economic recovery supports ORA demand, but consumer confidence remains fragile. New residents often use home sale proceeds to fund ORA entry costs.

Development pipeline depends on construction costs remaining manageable. Post-COVID construction inflation moderated but labour and materials costs are sticky. Fixed-price construction contracts partially mitigate this risk.

ORA resale gains and development margins depend on underlying property values. RBNZ rate cuts have supported some house price stabilisation (national sales volumes up ~10% in 2025), but ANZ lowered its 2026 house price inflation forecast to 2%, suggesting limited tailwind from capital appreciation in the near term.

Aged care is labour-intensive (employee costs $178m in FY25, ~68% of revenue). NZ has historically faced nursing shortages, although changes to overseas nurse certification pathways contributed to the closure of Wesley Institute. Current nursing oversupply has actually benefited retention metrics, but structural long-term shortage risk remains as demand for care grows.

execution.risk: Strategy transition risk (FY25-FY27 foundation to FY27-FY31 growth)
execution.description: Oceania must execute the near-term repair phase (sell down stock, reduce debt, cut costs, improve care profitability) while simultaneously positioning for the growth phase. Premature acceleration of development before the balance sheet is repaired could jeopardise financial stability.

Franklin is Oceania's first large-format greenfield broadacre development (ultimately 350+ units across multiple stages). Stage 1 (31 villas) is on track with 35.5% presales. Greenfield projects carry greater planning, construction, and sales risk than brownfield extensions.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The NZ retirement village and aged care sector has strong structural tailwinds. The 75+ population is expected to almost double by 2048-2050. NZ is projected to face a shortage of 12,000 aged care beds by 2032. The sector is simultaneously under financial pressure from government underfunding of care beds, creating urgency for operators to shift toward private-pay models. Budget 2025 provided $1.37bn per annum uplift in care funding. Industry growth rate for aged care residential services is 3-5% annually by volume, with premium retirement living growing faster. Consolidation is ongoing (Bupa NZ villages merged with Arvida).
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate - underlying demand for aged care is non-discretionary and demographically driven. However, the timing of ORA purchases is discretionary and correlates with NZ property market conditions. Development activity is highly cyclical in response to property markets and interest rates.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - both through direct financing costs (NZD $618m drawn debt) and through the NZ property market's effect on ORA demand and pricing. The RBNZ cutting OCR from 5.5% to 2.25% through 2025 is a meaningful tailwind. Bank debt average rate is 4.07%; retail bonds at 2.7% blended. A 1% increase in rates on variable bank debt would add ~$3.9m to annual interest costs.
macro_factors.nz_property_market: Moderate recovery underway. RBNZ OCR at 2.25% (February 2026 hold). National house price growth forecasts modest at 2-5% for 2026. Annual sales volumes rose 10.3% in 2025. Lower mortgage rates supporting affordability and ORA purchase financing. Auckland market particularly relevant given Oceania's heavy Auckland portfolio concentration.
macro_factors.government_funding_dependency: Care operations generate ~77% of operating revenue but a significant portion comes from government-subsidised beds (means-tested residents). Government funding rates are reset periodically. The July 2025 maximum contribution increases partially offset cost inflation. Oceania is actively reducing bed count and increasing care suite count to shift mix toward private-pay.

recent_developments.event: H1-FY2026 results: Proforma Underlying EBITDA $41.8m (+19.7% HoH), Operating Cash Flow $79.0m (+12.2%). Gearing reduced to 34.8%. $20.4m annualised cost savings programme on track. Care EBITDA per bed up 45.5% to $12.4k. No interim dividend declared; Board committed to resuming dividends when FCF from operations turns positive.

Investor Day held at Meadowbank Village, Auckland. Oceania unveiled 'Path to FY31' strategy, outlining FY26-FY27 foundation priorities and FY27-FY31 growth phase. Share price surged ~16% on the day. Annualised savings target of $20.4m confirmed. New dividend policy (40-60% of FCF from operations) announced at ASM.

New dividend policy announced at ASM in June 2025: targeting payout ratio of 40-60% of Free Cash Flow from Operations, replacing the previous 30-50% of Underlying NPAT policy. Dividends suspended until positive FCF from operations achieved.

Meadowbank Dementia Centre (40 dementia suites, the Orakei Building) opened in Auckland, completing the sixth and final stage of the Meadowbank Village redevelopment. 55% occupancy achieved within first four months.

FY25 full year results: Underlying EBITDA $86.0m (+4.1%), Operating Cash Flow $110.3m (+6.7%), Total Sales 520 units (+9.2%), Care occupancy 94.5% (excl. dev sites). Debt reduced to $627.8m. Banking facilities successfully refinanced with ANZ, ASB, ICBC and new lender BNZ, extending maturity profile.

Wesley Institute of Nursing Education closed after final course concluded. Decision taken due to changes in overseas nurse certification pathways reducing demand for NZ nursing education. Wesley had contributed ~$4.7m EBITDA in FY25.
Successful refinance of NZD $500m sustainability-linked syndicated bank facility, extended tenor, added BNZ as new lender, maintained existing covenants. Loan modification gain of $5.4m recognised.

Construction commenced at Franklin Village, Auckland (Oceania's first large greenfield broadacre development). Stage 1: 31 villas plus The Lodge community centre, targeting first residents January 2026. 35.5% presold as at November 2025. Additional 3.7ha purchased in September 2025 expanding Franklin to 11.6ha for 78 additional villas.

Suzanne Dvorak appointed CEO, replacing Brent Pattison. Dvorak brings aged care sector expertise and a sharper focus on operational delivery, people leadership, and financial discipline. Key personnel changes followed including new Chief Sales & Marketing Officer (November 2024) and elevation of Clinical function to executive level.

Divestment programme: Six non-core sites sold in FY25 for approximately $33.6m (Takanini, Holmwood, Middlepark, Victoria Place, Totara Park, Otumarama). A further four sites targeted for divestment in FY26 (~$40m expected proceeds). Programme reduces operational complexity and generates capital for debt repayment.

items.period: FY27 onwards (with $13.2m to be delivered in FY26)
items.notes: Originally $10-15m target (FY25 annual report). Subsequently raised to $20.4m by Investor Day September 2025. $4.0m delivered in 1HY26, $13.2m on track for full FY26.
Gearing 34.8% at 1HY26 (30 September 2025), within target range. Down from 36.3% at FY25 and 38.3% at FY24.
Target development rate once foundations are established. FY26 focus is primarily sell-down of existing stock. Franklin Stage 1 (31 villas) delivering January 2026.

items.metric: The Helier full development cash recovery
items.target: Full recovery of development costs by March-May 2026
items.notes: 54.5% occupied/under application as at 20 November 2025. Rate of applications has accelerated to 4 per month from October 2025 (vs less than 2 per month March-September). Based on 3-4 applications per month, full cash recovery expected March-May 2026.
Four sites targeted for completion in FY26 to release capital and reduce debt.

items.target: Return to positive FCF from operations
items.notes: 1HY26 FCF from operations was negative $(8.4)m but improved 30% on 1HY25. Dividends will resume when FCF is positive and sustainable. Management commentary suggests trajectory positive.
Care EBITDA per bed reached $12.4k in 1HY26 (up 45.5% HoH), with more than half of portfolio generating over $15.0k per bed per annum. Management expects this positive trajectory to continue.

items.target: 40-60% of Free Cash Flow from Operations
items.period: When FCF from operations is positive
items.notes: Previous policy was 30-50% of Underlying NPAT. New policy announced June 2025. No interim dividend for 1HY26. Dividends expected to resume when positive FCF from operations is sustainable.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Suzanne Dvorak: 'We have acted quickly and decisively as a leadership team. The progress over this focused period of execution ensures Oceania enters the next stage of its strategy with stronger cash generation, a leaner cost base, and the balance sheet strength to pursue disciplined, value-accretive growth. We said we'd strengthen sales, improve operational efficiency, and reduce debt. We're delivering on all three.' Chair Liz Coutts: 'Oceania is first strengthening its foundations to position the business for its next phase of growth. The longer-term strategic horizon (FY27-FY31) will build on these foundations, focusing on customer choice, service expansion, and future development.'

bull_case: Demographic inevitability: NZ's 75+ population doubling by 2048-2050, with a projected 12,000-bed shortage by 2032. Oceania's integrated care-village model directly addresses this structural demand. As the population ages, demand growth should accelerate regardless of economic conditions.

Care premiumisation inflection point: Care EBITDA per bed rose 45.5% in just one half to $12.4k, with more than half the portfolio now generating over $15k per bed. The shift from government-funded beds to private-pay care suites is a structural margin driver. If the full portfolio reaches $15k+ per bed, this alone could double care segment EBITDA.

Cost-out programme underappreciated: $20.4m annualised savings by FY27 represent a significant uplift on FY25 Underlying EBITDA of $86m (+24% incremental). Combined with care premiumisation, EBITDA could reach $110-120m by FY27 without any new development, creating significant EPS and FCF leverage.

Interest rate tailwind and property recovery: RBNZ cutting OCR to 2.25% reduces bank debt financing costs (saving ~$5-10m per annum vs peak rates) and supports the NZ property market, improving ORA demand and resale margins. Lower rates also reduce the opportunity cost for retirees of tying up capital in ORAs.

NTA discount provides valuation margin of safety: NTA per share of $1.57 (1HY26) versus current share price of c.$0.83 implies a 47% discount. If the business can demonstrate sustained FCF generation and debt reduction, a re-rating toward NTA is possible, offering significant upside. Analyst consensus price target of NZD $0.89-0.96 implies 7-15% upside from current levels, with some targets as high as $1.06.
bear_case: Debt burden limits strategic flexibility: Net debt of $609m against a market cap of c.$600-700m creates a highly leveraged capital structure. The development loan ($288m drawn vs $315m facility) is nearly fully utilised, constraining new development. Any deterioration in sales, property values, or care funding could threaten covenant compliance (ICR 2.5x vs 2.0x minimum) and force dilutive equity issuance.

The Helier and structural premium demand risk: Oceania's flagship luxury development has significantly underperformed sales expectations, with only 54.5% occupied/under application after more than 18 months. This raises questions about whether NZ has sufficient depth in the ultra-premium retirement market and whether future premium development projects will achieve targeted returns.

Retirement Villages Act reform could impair ORA model economics: Proposed mandatory buyback requirements (paying families while waiting for ORA resale) could materially increase working capital requirements, reduce the capital efficiency of the ORA model and pressure margins across the sector. The timing and severity of legislative changes remains uncertain.

Scale disadvantage versus Ryman and Summerset: Ryman Healthcare's vertically integrated model and Australian growth platform, and Summerset's strong customer satisfaction and growing portfolio, give these larger competitors sustainable advantages in brand, cost, and development pipeline. Oceania's smaller size makes it harder to invest in innovation, technology, and staff at the same rate.

FCF negative and dividends suspended: Free Cash Flow from Operations was negative $(8.4)m in 1HY26 and dividends have been suspended with no clear resumption timeline. Income-focused NZX investors may avoid the stock until dividend payments resume, limiting the potential buyer base and weighing on the share price relative to peers like Summerset that have maintained dividends.
